subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: That on and after Monday the 14th February, 1944, to the end of the present session, government ' notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence at every sitting over all other business except introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word in regard to this motion. I realize it follows the practice that prevails at- Westminster, and that in time of war, in the interests ,of the safety of the state, it is necessary to abrogate the rights of private members. Nevertheless, having regard to the fact that during the entire period of the last war, with the exception of the last four or five months, private

Precedence of Government Orders

members' days were left untouched. I again bring to the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the house the necessity of protecting the rights of private members. It is all very well to say that in Great Britain those rights have been taken away; but in Great Britain private members enjoy rights which are not granted to members of this house. Each day they have an opportunity of questioning the ministers of the crown, and if the ministers give unsatisfactory answers, supplementary questions are allowed. In any event the rights of the private members are protected in that at adjournment time they may again bring the question before the house.
I realize that the all-absorbing and exclusive business and responsibility of members of parliament is the mobilization of the nation for war and the making of plans for peace. As private members we have a great responsibility here. During the last few days statements have been made by members on the government side indicating an attitude in reference to parliament that [DOT] is far from encouraging. Our responsibility as members of parliament in connection with the war is to strengthen the resolution of the people to carry on to the end; to energize our people against the apathy that too often follows military successes; to assure our men and women of the forces that other men, with the necessary equipment, will be available as reinforcements and to see that our manpower is fully mobilized and put to the greatest possible use. For peace the challenge that comes to us as members is to make sure that the fullest possible plans and preparations be made now. I think I speak for the ordinary member of the house, Mr. Speaker, when I say that these aims and ideals for war and peace cannot be achieved if the membership of the house devotes itself, as it has to some extent during the past few days, to partisan discussions, and to turning this house into a cockpit of contending factions, each desirous of preparing for the hustings. Our responsibilities are too serious for that.
I ask the Prime Minister not to take away entirely the rights of private members. I realize that in time of war there must be a diminution in ordinary rights; that matters concerning the war must be given precedence; but we are living in times when parliament is losing its place in the opinion of the country. We are being criticized for wasting time; we are being criticized for abdicating two of our great functions, the deliberative and legislative functions. During this period
of war we have given up many of our privileges; we have put these things in pawn for victory. Private members are just as desirous as the government that we should get on with the business of the country, but we find our rights being whittled down, it is true with the consent of the house, until to-day we are almost in the position of being bound by the answers of the government. We cannot challenge the answers we get to questions asked on the orders of the day; we must accept what we are told. That is why ordinary members of parliament such as myself have reached the point where we feel that our rights should not be further curtailed.
Let me point out that this is not a partisan view I am expressing. The hon. member for Wellington South (M.r. Gladstone) dealt with this matter the other day, and two other hon. members are reported to have made speeches in the city of Hamilton last Saturday in connection with the same matter. I am not expressing a conception peculiar to the opposition. The hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Ross), referring to the labour order, is reported to have said:
The government is run by a bureaucracy; the members are nothing and I frankly admit it. If the order had gone through the house, it would have been better prepared.
Then the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Corman) as reported to have said:
The members of parliament are dead guinea pigs. I have never been consulted or called in on these matters. I admit there are powers behind the government. ... I think most of them are necessary, but I cannot see why the members should not be consulted. The Minister of Labour is not as bad as you think he is, but his hands are tied by these men who supposedly guide the destinies of this country.
Those are serious allegations against the power and prestige of the House of Commons. We find too that as time goes on the legislative authority of this parliament is being gradually diminished. No one can deny that. Orders in council of all kinds are necessary between sessions of parliament, but I submit that when parliament is sitting no orders in council should be passed at the instance of boards and commissions responsible only indirectly to parliament, carrying on uncontrolled by the representatives of the people, except those necessary for administrative purposes. We have only to look at the labour order to see what bureaucrats can do when they bring into effect legislation concerning the substantive rights of the individual, when there has been no discussion in parliament by the representatives of the people.
I realize the need to get on with the business of the war. Cn. the other hand, Mr. COMMONS
Precedence of Government Orders
Speaker, I say that private members should not be unnecessarily denied the privileges that are theirs. I appreciate the fact that for the first two or three months of the session the rights of private members must be abrogated; but I make the appeal that toward the end of the session at feast one day a -month be set aside as private members day. It may be argued that private members have -that opportunity in other ways, but I point out that -the same argument would apply in peace time. I am not one of those who believe that the importance of parliament is actually lessening. We have stood here together through dark days, but throughout the country the man on the street feels that we do not discharge our responsibilities. That is why I am offering this suggestion to-day, asking the Prime Minister, who has always stood as a proponent of the principles of parliamentary government, to protect the rights of the private members who, occupying no positions of power, nevertheless collectively have in our custody and care the rights of the people.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I whole-heartedly support what has been said by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). Year after year since the war began we have agreed to dispense with private members' days, but few opportunities are given hon. members to bring before this house ideas which they think would be beneficial to the country. If I remember correctly, last year we made a similar appeal to the Prime Minister, suggesting that while the government should get along with the business related to the war in the early part of the session, later on some opportunity should be given to private members to express their vie\jfs, and I-concur in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Lake Centre in that regard. I am particularly anxious that this should be emphasized this year because we are now approaching, we hope-I say, "we hope"- the time when we shall have to be giving closer consideration to the matters which will relate to the end of the war. If that is so, then it seems to me all the more important that private members, apart altogether from the legislation the government has foreshadowed, should be able from their places in the house to bring before parliament suggestions which they think might be beneficial to the country in the period which will follow.
I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre that if we were to study the opportunity given in the British parliament to private members, we would realize that we are more greatly restricted than are the members in what we sometimes call the mother of parliaments. As has already been said, they
IMr. Diefenbaker.]
have their question hour, at which time supplementary questions may be asked and ministers interrogated. They have also a custom which to my mind is an invaluable one, that of bringing matters to the attention of the house on the adjournment. A half hour is allotted to that daily. We have not that procedure here. As a consequence, sometimes hon. members have to take advantage of the motion to go into supply to bring some matter to the attention of the house, a procedure which often leads to long debate. Opportunities of that sort are few and far between, particularly in connection with appropriations made for war purposes, which in reality are a budget in themselves. I would urge the Prime Minister that he endeavour so to arrange the business of the house that, later in the session, when the pressure of war business has been eased somewhat, private members' days may be restored.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the resolution which I moved this afternoon is similar to those which have been approved by the house at each session of this parliament. The arguments made in support of it are, if anything, stronger to-day than they were at any preceding session. I am glad to see, therefore, that the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) both agree that there are reasons why, at least for the beginning of the session, the government should have an opportunity to get on with government measures, and that, if private members are to have an opportunity of bringing forward resolutions of their own, such opportunity should be postponed until later in the session. I think we are agreed on that.
So far as an opportunity being presented later in the session is concerned, I would say the government will be only too pleased to consider granting that opportunity in the light of conditions as they may develop. I did say in the last session that we would be prepared to consider giving private members an opportunity to bring forward resolutions when we got through the main part of our business. But I think all hon. members felt that by the time we reached the month of July they much preferred to have an adjournment of the house than to stay on for the purpose of debating the different motions placed on the order paper by private members.
Reference has -been made to the position at Westminster. I believe a comparison will show that in this house private members have an even greater opportunity of bringing forward

Precedence oj Government Orders
matters of interest to themselves, and of questioning the government, than is afforded at Westminster.
For instance, let us first consider the matter of questions, which has been mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre. He said that at Westminster the government can be questioned at considerable length. My understands ing of procedure there is that all questions to be answered by the government must be placed upon the order paper, and that the only questions which may be asked of the administration during the question hour are supplementary questions, growing out of those already asked. We adopt quite a different procedure here, one which gives hon. members a much greater opportunity to ask questions of the government. Almost every day the government is questioned in regard to some matter of which it has had no notice at all, and of which nothing whatsoever has appeared upon the order paper. On some days an hour's time is taken up in questions asked of the ministers. That would not be permitted under the procedure at Westminster. In this way, an opportunity does exist here for private members which does not exist in London. More than that, there is here no restriction upon the introduction of public bills by private members. In London during this time of war that right has been taken away from private members. They have not the right even to introduce a public bill.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: Of course our public bills do not get any further than the introduction stage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext:
Well, they do provide an opportunity to place before the public certain views which private members may wish to put forward. However,, the point I am emphasizing is this, that the government in taking its stand in this matter, and in making a request of the house, is not seeking to deprive private members of their rights. It is seeking to gain a high degree of cooperation on the part of hon. members in getting on with the all-important business, the business pertaining to the war. I am sure the leader of the opposition would recognize that fact if, on Monday next, the house were to begin a debate on some of the private members' motions; he would be the very first to say that the house had put itself in a false light before the public. The people of Canada would ask: Why is our parliament at this stage interesting itself in a number of motions which have been introduced by private members, instead of considering the war appropri-tion bill and other important war matters?
After all, what is the extent of the privation? In the first four weeks of the ordinary session hon. members have certain rights on Wednesdays and, I believe, Mondays. But after that government business has precedence.
In this session two weeks have already gone by, and hon. members have been perfectly free to discuss anything they liked, and have been under no restrictions whatsoever. The fact is that they have been discussing what they liked. We have had half a dozen amendments, apart from everything else, to the ' speech from the throne, and on them almost every subject of immediate concern has been discussed by one member or another. In those discussions there have been no restrictions whatsoever.
I do not like to have the impression develop in the public mind that private members have not full opportunity to discuss subjects in which they may be interested. The speech from the throne, we have been told, is lengthy.
It contains a number of subjects, each of which will come before the house in the course of the session. Hon. members may then address themselves to any of these questions.
Let us consider what would happen if we were to proceed now to a discussion of the private members' motions as they appear upon the order paper. The first of these motions is one which relates to measures for the better protection of all soldiers who serve in His Majesty's forces. There will be ample opportunity to discuss those matters on the war appropriation measure now to be proceeded with.
The next one has to do with the giving of clear titles to all soldier settlers who still hold land under contract with the soldier settlement board. That subject will come up under the estimates connected with soldier settlement, and in other connections.
The next resolution is one relating to reconstruction and rehabilitation; developments ensuring employment and opportunities in connection with transportation, and other matters. We shall be dealing at length with the whole question of reconstruction, and any member who wishes to discuss any particular phase of the subject will have his opportunity at such time.
The next resolution relates to the marketing of western Canada's wheat. My recollection is that in every session parliament has taken a couple of weeks to discuss wheat, and opportunities will come at such a time.
Next we find a resolution supporting feasible irrigation schemes in connection with post-war

Precedence of Government Orders
reconstruction. Such irrigation schemes can be discussed when we are dealing with the reconstruction measure.
Another has to do with the development of mineral resources under government control and operation. That, surely, would come up when we are discussing questions related to the resources of our country, and their development.
Finally there is a resolution relating to the prices of agricultural products. At other sessions we have discussed these matters, and ample opportunity will be given at this session for like discussion. And I suggest further that they will be much more effectively discussed when dealing with government measures on these subjects than they would be if discussed under private members' resolutions.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: May I ask a question? I hope the Prime Minister is not building up an argument for use after the war is over because actually what he is saying now about this resolution covering something that may be dealt with in the course of ordinary debate would apply equally to peace time. I hope the Prime Minister is not going to deny to private members in time of peace the opportunity of placing resolutions on the order paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for assuming that I will be directing the affairs of government at that time.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: I hope the war will be over very soon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: I am not at all surprised that my hon. friend should assume what he has, but let me say that the purpose of this resolution relates to war time only. There has been no attempt at any time that I am aware of to restrict private members' rights and privileges during a time of peace, by action similar to that being taken at this particular time because of the war.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: The same argument would apply to both peace and war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext:
The whole thought behind this resolution is that we are at war and that the country is interested in seeing that this parliament concentrates on the prosecution of the war, and regards everything else as secondary until victory has been achieved.
I might say more on this, but the house has passed a similar resolution in previous sessions and hon. members understand its purpose. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) has repeatedly made remarks, about

parliament losing caste with the people, private members being reduced to ciphers and comments of that kind. I cannot understand why he should go on trying to belittle parliament in the eyes of the public.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext:
Why deliver him a lecture
at this time?

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: Because he delivered a lecture to me.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: There was no question of any lecture. When the Prime Minister talks about-

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: -our prime purpose I would say to him that what I was talking about was the past two days when the Prime Minister's own supporters were doing anything but trying to win the war in the discussion that took place.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS AFTER FEBRUARY 14
speechtext: Seventy-five members have spoken during this debate, and I think if my hon. friend looks over the list he will find that there were comparatively few on this side who have participated. I do not want to go into any small discussion, but I have regard for the larger question, namely, the impression that the public may get with respect to parliament. I say that that impression may be created in two ways. First, it can be done by taking note of what actually has taken place in parliament and, second, by the iteration and reiteration of criticisms of its action by members of parliament themselves. I say that the latter kind of thing does no good either to parliament or to the public. My hon. friend has referred to the present session but I do not know of .any session of any parliament in Canada's history where more has been accomplished in the first two weeks after the opening of a session than has been accomplished in this session up to this time. Committees have been appointed, the speech from the throne has been agreed to, the estimates have been tabled, and there has been a full debate. If hon. members would direct the attention of the country to what has been accomplished in this way they would be serving a much better purpose than they are by criticizing adversely.
Motion agreed to.

ber for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) asked a question with respect to the present position of the extradition treaty with the United States, and I promised that I would have a statement to-day. If hon. members are agreeable, it might appear on Hansard, but I shall read it if it is desired.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
On January 29 of last year I informed the house that the government had received representations from many organizations in Canada which are interested in the marketing of securities and which feared possible adverse effects from the treaty upon legitimate Canadian business. I informed the house that these representations were being given careful study.
Since making the statement to which I have referred, a hearing was held on May 18 last before a special committee of the cabinet consisting of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), and the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), at which all organizations and individuals interested in the possible effects of the treaty were given an opportunity to make any representations they wished concerning the treaty. Following that hearing, the whole matter was discussed informally with the security commissioners of all the provinces in the course of meetings held in Winnipeg at the end of May. Following these discussions, representatives of the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Justice proceeded to Washington to have further consideration of the position with the United States authorities.
The position at present is that discussions are going on between the Canadian and United States governments as to the nature and extent of any modification which it might be desirable to make in the effect of the treaty in order to ensure that no legitimate business operations are affected by its terms. It is hoped that it will be possible to conclude these discussions very shortly and to have the matter placed before parliament for approval. Such approval will be sought before ratification of the treaty is proceeded with. The treaty was tabled in the house by the Minister of Justice on August 1, 1942.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF ORDER WITH RESPECT TO THE USE OF TRUCKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance in regard to a recent order of the wartime prices and trade board forbidding the use of trucks for so-called "wasteful or unnecessary purposes". During

the last month or so there have been a number of prosecutions against farmers for attending social or church gatherings in their trucks, even though they have no other means of transport. My question is this: Will consideration be given by the government to having that order altered so as to permit farmers and others who have no other means of conveyance than the truck to attend social or church gatherings without rendering themselves subject to prosecution and conviction?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. C. ABBOTT (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF ORDER WITH RESPECT TO THE USE OF TRUCKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend was good enough to give me notice of his question. We have had similar inquiries from a number of other hon. members. As my hon. friend knows, the substance of the order forbids the wasteful and unnecessary use of gasoline used in going to and from social gatherings, recreation meetings and so on. The underlying purpose is to conserve trucks, gasoline, and rubber, which is still in very short supply. When the amending order No. 318 was passed last September, careful consideration was given to whether or not an exception could be made for the owners of trucks who were not the owners of pleasure vehicles. However, the gasoline ration for trucks is more than double, I think, the ration for the ordinary pleasure vehicle, and in addition gasoline and new tires can be obtained, if necessary, for trucks. So that after consideration it was felt that to make such an exception would contravene the fundamental purpose of the order. I shall be glad to bring my hon. friend's question to the attention of the officers of the board, but the information I now have is that it is unlikely that any change will be made in the order at the present time.

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, inter alia,
1.	That sums not exceeding $3,650,000,000 be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending March 31, 1945, for-
(a)	the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
(b)	the conduct of naAfal, military and air operations in or beyond Canada;
(c)	promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever; and
(d)	the carrying out of any measures deemed necessary or desirable by the governor in council in consequence of the existence of a state of war.
2.	That the governor in council be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, such sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of $3,650,000,000 as may be required for the purpose of defraying such expenses or making such advances or loans, the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.
3.	That the governor in council be empowered to reexpend, advance or loan moneys that may be received by way of refund or repayment of advances, loans or expenditure under the War Appropriation Acts of 1939 (second session), 1940, 1941, 1942, 1943 and 1944.
He said: You will note, Mr. Speaker, that this resolution asks for authority to introduce a bill which is designed to provide the appropriation we shall require for war expenditures during the new fiscal year which begins on April 1 next. Except in regard to the amount asked for, the resolution is in exactly the same form as on previous occasions; and similarly the house will find that, with the same exception, the bill itself, Avhen introduced, will be in exactly the same form as the main war appropriation bill introduced at the last session of parliament.

War Appropriation-Mr. Ilsley
This will be the tenth appropriation for direct war expenditures which parliament has been asked to provide during the present war. It may therefore be of some historical interest if I review the previous appropriations. The house will note that I am speaking of appropriations to cover only Canada's direct war expenditures; I am not including the appropriations for indirect war purposes, that is to say, appropriations to provide munitions and other war supplies to our allies.
At the first war session in September, 1939, parliament voted a war appropriation of $100 million. War expenditures during the fiscal year 1939-40 amounted to $118 million, the remainder of the funds being supplied from the ordinary vote of the Department of National Defence which had been included in the ordinary estimates for the fiscal year.
In May, 1940. parliament appropriated $700 million for direct war expenditures during the fiscal year 1940-41, and on April 4, 1941, voted a supplementary appropriation of $135 million. Direct war expenditures during the fiscal year 1940-41 charged to these two votes amounted to $752,045,000.
The main war appropriation for the fiscal year 1941-42 amounted to $1,300 million, and had to be supplemented by a further vote of $135 million in March, 1942. Direct war expenditures during the year totalled $1,339,-
700,000.
For the fiscal year 1942-43, three war appropriation acts were passed, one for $500 million in March, 1942, one for a further $1,500 million in June, 1942, and the third for $858 million at the end of the year. Total direct war expenditures during the fiscal year amounted to $2,724,200,000.
These eight votes for direct war expenditures total $5,22S million. Total direct war expenditures to the end of the last fiscal year, March 31, 1943, aggregated $4,934 million, to which should be added loans and advances charged to active assets, of $144 million, making a grand total of $5,078 million. This figure excludes indirect war expenditures to provide war supplies to other united nations.
For the present fiscal year, the house will recall that we passed last spring a main war * appropriation act for $3,890 million-in addition, of course, to the Mutual Aid Act appropriating $1,000 million for the provision of war supplies to other united nations. We are still too far from the end of the fiscal year for me to forecast with any accuracy to-day the probable total of our direct war expenditures for the present fiscal year. However, 'I am hoping that when the accounts for the
year are closed, we will find that actual expenditures for the year have run very close indeed to the original estimate we made and that no further funds for this purpose will have to be voted by parliament. Parenthetically, I may add that I expect the mutual aid appropriation of $1,000 million to carry expenditures for mutual aid purposes several weeks beyond the end of the fiscal year.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the appropriation which parliament is being asked to provide for the coming fiscal year, namely $3,650 million, is somewhat smaller than the provision which was made for direct war purposes for the current fiscal year. Actually the decrease is $240 million, or slightly over six per cent. I need not assure the house that this probable reduction in direct war expenditures, like the corresponding decrease forecast by President Roosevelt in connection with United States war expenditures, does not represent any slackening in the war effort but rather merely the result of the stage of the war and of our preparation for war which has now been reached. The speech from the throne clearly indicated that while the war situation has improved from the point of view of the united nations during the past year, nevertheless the duty of the government is to see that Canada's war effort is firmly maintained until the enemy is defeated in Europe and in Asia. The winning of the war clearly remains the first of all our objectives. The primary task of the government and of the Canadian people is to concentrate on the prosecution of the war and assure our men in the armed forces that there will be no diversion from this vital task and no relaxation of Canada's war effort until victory is conclusively won.
Despite the reduction, the vote asked for is still a huge one,, judged by any Canadian standard. Its magnitude and the fact that it is to provide for our direct war financial programme for the new year makes the war appropriation bill the most important by far of the many measures with which the house will have to deal during the present session. As in previous years, the resolution and the bill itself will provide ample opportunity for discussing and appraising not only the war programme which we are proposing for next year but also the record of war activities and war expenditures during the fiscal year now drawing to a close. It will be the purpose of my colleagues and myself to afford full opportunity to hon. members to make such inquiries and
IFar Appropriation-Mr. llsley

comments as they may wish to make, and to give them pertinent information in as complete a form as may be practicable.
To facilitate such inquiries and debate, I will now place on Hansard a break-down, by the main categories of expenditure in the form used last year, of the estimated expenditure of $3,650 million for the fiscal year 1943-44. For the convenience of the house, I am also showing in the same table the corresponding estimates for the current fiscal year. Unfortunately, as I have already indicated, I find it impracticable to be responsible for giving, in addition, estimates of probable actual expenditures under each item during the current fiscal yean, but I have no doubt that my colleagues
will be prepared to report actual expenditures to some recent date and perhaps also will be willing to hazard rough estimates of probable total expenditures for the various items which come within their own jurisdiction.
The table showing the break-down of the estimated war expenditures for 1944-45 to which I have referred is too long to read, and if the house will permit me I will merely place it on Hansard and then direct attention to some of its major features and the more important items.

Yes. When hon. members have an opportunity to examine the table they will note that in round numbers the aggregate expenditures of the three defence services are estimated at S3,057 million as compared with the original estimate of S3,405 million given for the current fiscal year. Breaking down these totals, we find that army services account for SI,535 million in 1944-45 as compared wTith $1,764 million in 1943-44; air services SI,090 million as compared with SI,129 million; naval services $410 million as compared with S4S9 million; and sundry services $22-3 million as compared with $22-5 million.
As I have already indicated, these somewhat smaller figures in each case reflect primarily the stage which we have now reached in the war itself and in our preparations for war. In other words, we have at long last reached, or at least nearly reached, the end of the costly period of preparation for total war, the end of the discouragingly long period during which we, like other peace-loving nations, have been trying to "catch up" in trained man-power, in armoured strength, and in the capacity for making the weapons for war with an enemy who had devoted several years to war-like preparations before he finally "struck" and who had therefore caught us largely unprepared. For the united nations, therefore, the initial years of war were primarily years of holding the enemy at bay by rapidly improvised programmes while we reorientated our whole economy, built new plants and extended old ones for war purposes, mobilized our man-power and trained it in the new technique of modem war and war industry, and gradually built up supplies of initial and reserve equipment considered adequate to knock out a powerful and resourceful enemy already armed to the teeth.
Fortunately, as I have said, we have reached or are reaching the point, varying to some extent in varying fields of equipment and activity, when, thanks to the superiority of our industrial resources and the resourcefulness which characterizes the democratic organization of the united nations, we can deliver against the enemy that overpowering weight of armed power which is essential for assuring victory as well as for minimizing the loss of human lives. What I have been saying applies to the united nations as a group as well as to Canada; for this tremendous mobilization for war against the common enemy has been a cooperative process involving mutual help and the integration of resources of the several nations to a very high extent. Had such
cooperation and mutual assistance been lacking, the period of preparation to which I have referred would have taken much longer- perhaps indeed the victory we aim at could not otherwise have been achieved.
The huge war appropriation which this parliament voted last year represented in a very real way the harvesting of much of this prolonged work of preparation. The very large increases in the sums then made available to our three defence services, as compared with those provided in preceding years, were to enable them to fill up their quota of initial equipment and build up reserves as far as practicable. The somewhat smaller sums being asked for this year reflect to a substantial degree the fact that this process is nearing completion and that what is now primarily necessary is to provide equipment and supplies to repair the wastage of equipment and supplies that will accrue in a period of more intense and more continuous war activity, and to keep constantly abreast or ahead of the enemy in the development and provision of new and better weapons which the changing phases of the war require. To some extent also it reflects the completion or near-completion of the construction programme of the three services.
The Department of Munitions and Supply, which is the procurement agency for the defence services as well as for other allied governments in respect of Canadian war supplies, estimates its requirements for the coming fiscal year at S183 million. This compares with the estimate of $166,300,000 for the current fiscal year which I gave for this department at the beginning of the year, although I understand that the funds actually required by this department will, because of working capital requirements, be found to have substantially exceeded this estimate.
For the war activities carried on by all other departments or agencies of government, the estimate for 1944-45 is roughly $375 million as compared with the estimate of approximately $249 million for the present fiscal year. Of this total the two largest single items are $156-6 million for administrative expenses of and subsidies to be paid by the commodity prices stabilization corporation, and approximately S74 million for the Department of Agriculture (including almost $47,600,000 for subsidies to food producers paid through the agricultural food board, $16,500,000 freight assistance on western feed grains, and $8,000,000 subsidy on western wheat used exclusively as feed for live stock). The amounts estimated for other departments are of much
War Appropriation-Mr. Ilsley

smaller magnitude and compare more closely with the corresponding estimates for the current year.
Finally, there is an estimate of S30-5 million as the amount required to cover cash outlays charged to active assets rather than to expenditure, leaving a small amount for contingencies.
The minister has not the total of subsidies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The total estimated subsidies will be apparent from the tables I placed on Hansard.
I shall not at this time say more about the details of these estimates by departments and functions. As I said last year, to do so would be needlessly confusing to the house, because it has not vet had time to study and digest the salient features of the table which I have placed on Hansard.
It also seems to me unnecessary to dwell at length on the general economic and financial significance of the over-all figures and it is too early for me to present to the house an accurate picture of our probable total expenditures for all purposes during the coming fiscal year.
The main estimates, which I have tabled to-day, show an increase, due primarily to increased interest on the public debt, but on the other hand we expect to be able to effect a considerable reduction in the appropriation which it will be necessary to request for mutual aid purposes. The global figure for government expenditures for all purposes during the coming year is therefore expected to be smaller than the total which parliament appropriated for all purposes during the present fiscal year.
In commenting upon the general significance of the sum requested for direct war expenditures, I wish to emphasize again that it is based on the assumption that Canada wishes to maintain a total war effort-wishes to make the maximum contribution of which it is capable during the coming year to the achievement of victory. That, I believe, represents the point of view of this house and of the country generally. The vast majority of hon. members and of the Canadian people do not wish it to be said of this country that we fought a "comfortable" war-that we stopped short of doing the most we could do to assure victory and, moreover, assure it at the earliest possible moment and with the least possible sacrifice of human lives. On the contrary,
I think they will wish to look back on their record in this war in the way that Walter Lippmann looked back to the record of the (Mr. Ilsley.]
united nations during the past year. Let me quote from what he wrote on the eve of the new year:
The year which lies behind us will in the perspective of time be remembered proudly and gratefully. . . .
The nations have been put to the test and they have met the test. Facing defeat, they have not despaired. Confronted with impossible tasks, they have accomplished them. In the judgment of history there will stand forth the grand result, and not the trouble and confusion by which we have reached it. . . .
We may say with sober confidence that we shall have the victory and that we shall come through the ordeal into one of the great epochs of human history. We have faced fearful danger and a monstrous evil; let us not be too timid to believe that in the certain triumph of this righteous cause our children will find peace and the good life again.
Our assurance that this is so rests upon the proved fact that for the greatest things in this enormous conflict-for resistance to evil, for the courage to fight, for patience to wait, the resolution to work, the readiness to endure 

our people have not been wanting. It is in the incidental and secondary things that we have been least successful.
I do not contend that everything that he says is applicable to Canadian conditions, athough some of it is. He continues:
The nagging contentions which disgust us and disgrace us have not been about the central and mighty issues of this momentous struggle. The contentions have been about seventeen cents an hour and two cents a quart for milk, and a few dollars of taxes, and a little more or a little less profit on a war contract; the contentions have been about ivho should stay in a public office or who should replace him, and how to finagle to stay in and how to manoeuvre to get in. These are the small change of the small transactions of small men who live in the little private worlds of their personal grievances and their private ambitions, *while the majestic drama of the great world, which alone can give purpose and meaning to any human life to-day, passes them by. . . .
The great things are going well, and they have been made to go well by thought and work and faith, not by accident and good luck.
There are, I am convinced, very few Canadians who wish to live meaninglessly in comfort or luxury while "the majestic drama of the great world" passes them by; few who fail to realize that we as individuals get out of life what we put into it and we as nations will share in "the grand result" of this struggle in proportion to the contribution we have made towards it. It is true that there were one or two voices raised in this house w'hich have condemned Canada's war effort on the alleged ground that it is "out of proportion to our resources" and indeed-believe it or not- that it is "proportionately greater than that of any other allied country." The facts, I think, speak for themselves. The fact is that our war effort cannot be too big, for the simple reason

War Appropriation-Mr. Graydon
that we have been been able to accomplish it. It is a travesty of truth to say that it is proportionately greater than that of any other allied country. We have done well for a small and youthful country; we have done more than the world thought we could do and more indeed than we ourselves ever dreamed that we could do, but he makes a mockery of words who says that our effort and our sacrifices are proportionately greater than the achievements and the sacrifices of the heroic people of Britain and of Russia, or the nameless suffering of the peoples of the conquered countries.
What have we in Canada suffered or sacrificed? I speak not of our fighting men or of families who have lost their loved ones. I speak only of those of us who have remained at home and are supposed to support the home front. Well, the fact is that we have suffered a few inconveniences and sacrificed some chance of profit that fattening on the extremities of other nations might otherwise have brought to us. But when you have said that, you have said all. For the nation as a whole the standard of living has risen substantially, and again on the whole it is higher than it has ever been before. Our national income has risen to unprecedented heights and it is distributed far more equitably than ever before. True, our national debt is also far higher than ever before but the significant thing is that when we take into account lower interest rates and other offsetting factors, we find that the annual burden created by that debt, the net interest charge, is smaller in relation to national income and taxable capacity than the burden of the national debt before the war or even twenty years ago. That debt will create its problem of management, no doubt, but that problem will be by no means beyond our capacity to solve. The key to it will be found in the maintenance of a high level of employment., production and national income.
To that objective we are committed. I have no doubt of our ability to achieve it, if we show boldness and intelligence in our planning and do not allow our constructive efforts to be frustrated by bickering and Strife. Fortunately, thanks to the fact that we have conceived our war effort in great and noble proportions, we shall go into the post-war period with many new assets. In particular, we shall have a vastly expanded and more highly diversified industrial equipment, a wide range of newly-acquired skills, a larger, better-trained and healthier population, and a new sense of achievement, a new confidence in our capacity to do great and difficult things. Some of these assets are of an intangible character but they are of the first importance for the tasks that will face us.
Neither now in planning our war effort nor later in planning for the new and better world which we hope it will make possible can we afford to be timid or selfish or short-sighted. We cannot afford to take counsel of small minds or selfish hearts. We must seek to do our best, the utmost of which we are capable.
That is the philosophy which has guided us in planning the war programme which requires the appropriation for which we are now asking. That programme is large and varied, but it is one which we believe we can accomplish.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the house resolving .itself into committee to deal with the war appropriation resolution. I rise simply to repeat what I said last session when I indicated to the minister and the government our desire to have before us the details of the expenditures proposed for the further prosecution of the war. The Minister of Finance has now tabled the details for this year.
We are anxious this year, as we were last session, to discharge our obligation and our duty as members of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition. We intend to see that the money which has been raised by taxation, by loan and otherwise is spent to the best advantage. At this moment I think I should caution and warn the government that we are taking a definite stand with respect to war expenditures. The government may expect a closer and more effective scrutiny of each item in the war appropriations than was given last year. There are more people who are conscious of the expenditures of our government. More people in Canada are pay'ing taxes than ever before, and when a man pays taxes his consciousness of public expenditures becomes that much greater.
It will be a strange thing if there is not great waste and great extravagance in certain parts of our effort. Perhaps that, may have been expected in the hurly-burly and hurry of the early stages of the war, to which the minister has alluded, but now an entirely different set. of circumstances exists. The plan and the chart and the course of the war are known to the government. They have their organization in shape to handle the vast enterprises they are now conducting, and there is not the same reason why there should be any evidence of waste or extravagance in connection with the prosecution of Canada's national effort. Again I caution the government, and particularly the Minister of Finance and the other ministers charged with departments directly concerned with the prosecution of the war, that we shall accept nothing less than the fullest information,

War Appropriation-Mr. ColdweU.
freely and willingly given in reply to the inquiries that we shall put from time to time in the committee stage. We are not desirous of continuing this general debate because we feel that the interests of Canada can best be protected and advanced by allowing the resolution to proceed into committee as soon as possible.
There is an additional reason why I think that at this time neither the house nor the country would wish that time be spent unnecessarily in a general discussion. This nation has been awaiting for some considerable time answers to certain questions which have been put more particularly to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). He is here in the house and ready, I understand, to go ahead with his estimates under the war appropriation. I think myself that we have already waited too long for the information he is about to give to the committee when we reach that stage. We are desirous of fulfilling our obligations as an opposition by giving the closest possible scrutiny to every dollar of expenditure which the government is making in the prosecution of the war. Our people do not mind raising the money by whatever means may be necessary, but there is at the same time a corresponding demand on the part of every taxpayer in Canada that we see to it that the money that is raised is properly and efficiently and economically spent, even in the hurry and haste of war. That is something that the taxpayer of Canada has the right to expect. That is something which we here, as members of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition, will endeavour to accomplish by scrutiny, audit and investigation of the accounts.
In taking my seat I want it distinctly understood that I do so not for the purpose of hurrying this resolution into committee but rather because we feel that by facilitating the business of the house in this way we shall the sooner be able to deal with the indivdiual items, which after all are the most important part of the discussion which will follow.
May I before I sit down ask the Minister of Finance two questions. I would have done so while he was on his feet but I was intrigued particularly by the latter part of his address and I did not wish to interrupt him. I should like to know, and I think the country would like to know how much this government intends to appropriate for Mutual Aid during the coming year. I do not think the minister gave that although he came very close to it on one occasion.
I should also like to know the government's plans with respect to the procedure that will be followed in committee. Are we going to follow the same procedure as last year? So far

there has been no agreement, as I understand it, among the different parties with respect to the procedure to be followed in discussing the war appropriation resolution this year. I think it is a proper inquiry for me to make in order that we may find out in what sequence the departments will be taken up when we get into committee.

Mr. Speaker, we are not yet in committee, and I do not want it to be understood that if the minister now replies to the questions just asked he will be closing the debate, because I do not wish to lose the privilege of saying a word or two.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with the consent of the house I can answer the questions now, although we are not in committee. The amount of the Mutual Aid appropriation has not yet been agreed upon. If it were I could state the overall estimate for our total expenditures for the coming year, which I am not yet quite prepared to do. I know what I think the Mutual Aid will be but I do not wish to announce it until I am sure. All I can say is that it will be less than last year.

Less than a billion
dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, less than a billion. My hon. friend's other question was as to the procedure this year. I propose that the procedure shall be exactly the same as last year, that the departments be taken up in rotation.
In the same rotation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will take the defence departments first. I do not know about the other departments. There might be some variation there; I have not given any thought to that. At present I can see no reason why they should not be taken up in the same rotation, except that, by agreement, some department might be taken up in advance of another that was expected to be taken up at a particular time. The intention is to follow the procedure of last year.

Mr. Speaker, we have all listened with a great deal of interest to the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). Whether or not we agree with his views on social and economic matters, we all respect him and realize that he gives close attention to the work of his department and carries his heavy task with a good deal of honour to himself and to this house.
The expenditure this year, he has said, will be smaller than that of last year, but it is still ten million dollars a day-a very large sum of money for Canada when stated in those terms. We of this party are agreed

War Appropriation-Mr. Blackmore
that whatever is required of us to wiu the war should be given without stint, and we are prepared to support the government in all that is necessary in order to carry on the great struggle against the forces which are threatening the freedom of the world.
I did not rise at this stage to discuss the resolution but rather to say a word about the procedure to be followed. The war appropriation is, after all, the biggest budget that this house has to consider during the course of the year-many times larger than the civii budget which we shall adopt later in the session. In looking over the records of the last few years I find that this main appropriation is passed in the form of a bill; the bill becomes an act, and it is unlike any other budgetary act because it has not attached to it the schedules of expenditures. This afternoon I sent for a copy of the new edition of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms. At page 168, paragraph 439, dealing with a money resolution, it is stated:
The object of the resolution recommended by the crown is to give the bouse a first opportunity to discuss the advisability of making a certain expenditure. The details of the projected measure are not then disclosed and debate is confined to the resolution which should not be lengthy, although care must be taken that the terms used are sufficiently wide to cover the whole of the bill which will be subsequently introduced.
That is the procedure laid down by the rules of this house. I have thought for some time that the procedure we have followed and apparently are to follow again this year is irregular; it does not conform with the rules. I would not object to irregularity where it served a useful purpose, but in regard to these large expenditures, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) said a few moments ago, we should exercise care, scrutinize every expenditure, and adequately protect this nation. Consequently it seems to me that what we should be doing this afternoon is saying to the minister: Yes; we approve the principle of the resolution; let us pass it into committee and recommend its adoption as quickly as possible, so that we may examine the bill to be founded upon it. In short, we should discuss in detail the bill, not the resolution. That has been the procedure of this parliament from time immemorial. We should not be discussing the resolution for days or weeks; we should be discussing the bill and the schedules attached thereto. If the present procedure is allowed to remain as a precedent, it will be a very bad one. I raise the question this afternoon in the hope that the various groups in the house will be able to agree with the Minister of Finance
that we dispose quickly of the resolution stage and get down to the actual consideration of the war appropriation estimates when the bill is before us. Let us follow the proper parliamentary procedure and ask the government to bring down a bill at the earliest convenience, say on Monday next.

I believe that every hon. member looked back with a measure of regret on our performance last year with respect to the war appropriation bill. We spent far too long in more or less rambling and aimless discussions of questions upon the various items which were listed for us in the break-down of the appropriations to the various ministers. In my view that waste of time, or shall I say unwise expenditure of time, resulted largely from the way in which we went about the whole thing. I believe that if the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) were adopted, we would save a great deal of time and be much better satisfied after the whole thing was over.
I believe that all hon. members, and I am sure all hon. members of my group, are fully in accord with winning this war and fully prepared to support the minister to any extent that he deems advisable in carrying on the war. If three and one-half billion dollars are sufficient for him, good; if he asked for more we would support him for that higher figure. I do wish therefore that we could get the resolution off our hands and have the bill before us so that we could discuss the whole matter with much more accuracy and effectiveness.

I agree with what the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldwell) said with regard to bringing in a bill at once and not having a double-barrelled or futile discussion of the resolution itself.
Bearing upon the answer which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) gave to the leader of the opposition (Mr. .Graydon) with regard to the amount of Mutual Aid to be brought down this year, and apropos of his statement that the matter was still under review, that it would not exceed the allowance of last year, but had yet to be determined, if I am in order in so doing I would offer for the consideration of the Minister of Finance and his colleagues the suggestion that we should entirely eliminate an allowance by way of mutual aid this year. No other of the commonwealth nations makes any such allowance. Our own contribution in maintaining our own armed forces and our other obligations is heavy indeed. We can be proud of that, aside from an additional
War Appropriation-Army

mutual aid allowance. There are many reasons, in my view, to support that suggestion, but now is not the proper time to give them to the house.
I desire to be understood as not including in my objection a special allowance which Canada will be asked to make this year to the organization known as UNNRA, or a contribution with our other allies to feed the starving conquered nations. I think that is an obligation, and that we must make an appropriate contribution; but, except for that, I desire with the greatest respect to suggest to the minister the entire elimination of an allowance for mutual aid.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
A year ago, when I spoke in the
house on a similar occasion, I talked about preparation of the army. I now can speak of accomplishments. When I spoke last year the clearing of North Africa had just been completed. I said that the year ahead looked like a year of action, and that if it was the Canadians would be in the thick of events for which plans and preparations had been under way. I said that they were on a front which would in all likelihood prove to be the decisive front of the war. I said that they might fight on that front or on some other; that they might fight as an army or in separate formations; that wherever they were they would be a power to be reckoned with just as Canadians were twenty-five years ago.
To-day the army overseas finds itself on two fronts and I want to speak very briefly first of the troops in the Mediterranean area and of the visit which I made there in November and December. I have made no report to anybody with regard to it except to my colleagues in the government; but I think it is due our soldiers themselves and perhaps due the house that I say just a few words regarding what I saw. I spent three weeks there. I think I saw something of everything. I wished I could have seen everybody. It is not possible to take the house on a day-to-day tour, but I want to do a little more than generalize. I am afraid that half-and-half narrative may prove a dull resume of what was a trip with not a dull moment in it.
I saw the troops in three areas: North Africa, Sicily and Italy. I was in North Africa first and then in Italy, then back to Sicily, then back to Italy again, then back to Sicily and then to North Africa. The troops at that time were distributed, with reinforcements in North Africa and a hospital there. The corps troops

were in Sicily with another hospital there, and two divisions were in Italy with hospitals there. I have described the terrain to the people of Canada in something said over the radio from Campobasso. I can only repeat that it is terrain such as I never saw before, and I do not think many of us who were in the last war have seen battle conditions such as I saw in Italy. There were hills in ceaseless succession, longitudinal roads few and far between, narrow winding roads up hills toward the towns on top which had to be taken, and a wonderful opportunity of which full advantage was taken by the enemy in the use of mines on the hair-pin turns and for demolition of bridges.
As I say, I saw first the reinforcements in North Africa. I was there just two days. The troops in North Africa felt they were a long distance away from the war and their one idea and eagerness was to get further forward. They have been moved since then. I saw their hospital under field conditions. It is a hospital with over eleven hundred patients under canvas, operating under what were truly battle conditions without any actual fighting. It was on a hillside. The canvas had been blown down repeatedly. Cooking had to be done on the top of the hill and food carried something like a quarter of a mile in containers to the patients who were in marquees. I found that the hospital had been operating at that time for nearly five months with the highest morale, the greatest energy and the finest efficiency that one could imagine.
Then I went to Italy and saw the forward troops first. I saw the armoured troops disposed on each side of the road, some in billets, but many of them sleeping out in pup tents. I talked to these men as I went along. I remember the first headquarters I visited and the first group to which I spoke. At that time a lump came into my throat as I realized what those men had gone through, because I knew that particular formation and how all the way from Pachino up they had shown their worth.
There I learned what we have' to learn in this war, that operations are conducted to no small extent by means of task forces. By that I mean forces which are not necessarily homogeneous in the matter of the particular country from which the troops come or homogeneous in the particular arm of the service to which they happen to belong. The forces are put together because of the teamwork which the various arms of the services can do, and which various men from various countries can do in a combined operations to deal with a particular situation, having regard to the disposition of the enemy, the communications, the terrain, and the ultimate objective. They do not use an armoured brigade when

IFar Appropriation-Army
they can use a battalion; they detach the battalion if necessary for that purpose to make up the force which does the job. That, after all, is what counts. That is happening in the Mediterranean area constantly and is happening more in this war than ever before- the combination of troops from various countries and the combination of various arms of the services in task forces rather than in more normal organization of divisions, corps and armies. That armoured formation of ours had been in all sorts of operations as sometimes doing a task with the British and sometimes with our own division.
When I saw the armoured corps one battalion was not there, and I saw it afterwards, a battalion which had made a magnificent reputation for itself. After seeing the armoured corps I saw the forward troops. I was at one battalion headquarters where they had had a pretty tough time a couple of nights before. They had lost some men. They had sent a detachment to capture a strong feature in front of an important town. They had had to retire and to reorganize. They had sent in another detachment and captured and held the position, and were just as proud ns if they had taken Rome itself. They were living under conditions which wore pretty grim. There were no funk-holes, no trenches and no dug-outs such as veterans of the last war know. They were out in the open under the cold Italian stars with nothing but the groundsheet between them and the cold earth.
I was thrilled by my visit with them. There I learned the fluidity of the so-called line and the fluid and constantly moving nature of the operations. No over-the-top attack at dawn by a line of soldiers getting out of a trench, but fighting done by patrols fighting forward, capturing a post, moving in, then another patrol coming up and capturing another post and so on, zigzagging back and forth, finally getting toward the objective until the time comes when the guns put on the intensive bombardment, and then the assault. On that front that was going on constantly. One could not tell really just where the front was, made up as it was by patrols and by posts.
Then I saw the rear division, first the infantry brigade and later the armoured brigade, keen, anxious, alert, wanting very much to get forward, wondering how long it would be before they would be in the battle area. I knew some of the units, and I was impressed more than I can say with the sturdiness, with the appearance of good health, and with their evident determination to do their part and to keep up the fine record which our first division had established.
I visited the reinforcements in Italy, in perhaps the most attractive town I saw there. It was a touch of home to see, up on one of Mussolini's recreation centres, the sign "Maple Leaf Gardens." The streets of that town are given Canadian names. I visited another town where divisional headquarters was located at that time, where they had the Beaver club and where, by the way-and this is not intended to advertise the Canadian Pacific railway-they also had the Royal York hotel. That was a regular Canadian town. On the streets were hundreds of Canadian soldiers from the support brigades billeted in the nearby villages. They came in for a show and a day off after a strenuous tour up front. I visited, in that one day, I think ten units of the two support brigades, and had an opportunity of saying a word to them, bringing them greetings from Canada, and of bringing messages back from them. I want to say to hon. members that I have never had a more inspiring or more exhilarating or more stimulating experience. They were well turned out, clear eyed, earnest, sure of themselves because they had "been there." I saw the corps troops; they were in Sicily. The second morning before I left the word was going round over the "clothes-line" telegraph that Hitler had capitulated. Everybody was sore; they said this was a phoney war, that they had been sent to Italy when we knew there was no action going on there. That was the story, and they did not like it a bit. I am only sorry to say that since then many of those boys have learned the lesson that many of us in Canada have to learn; that is, that the war is not over and that Hitler has not capitulated. Many stem battles have been fought by those men since I saw them.
I saw another hospital in Sicily, excellently located. They had made a name for themselves in the early days of the fighting. They had lost all their equipment, but with captured German hospital equipment they had set up their establishment and, although they only had about 300 beds, they cleared something like 3,300 patients in sixteen days.
I should have said that I saw in Italy other hospitals, one of which had arrived at its location only the day before, had established itself in a practically new Italian hospital, and had already opened one wing with over 50 patients.
The nurses, medical officers, and personnel of another hospital I visited had been through a trying experience. Their ship was torpedoed and, although fortunately there was not a single casualty, they had lost everything in the way of personal belongings. However by a stroke of luck their hospital equipment was on
40S
War Appropriation-Army

another ship, and they expected to be in a position to take 200 patients within two days after I was there.
Finally I visited the assembly place of the dead who fell in Sicily, the cemetery near Agira, looking up at that town which one Canadian brigade captured with such marvellous courage and such dauntlessness in an operation that had been delayed^ a day behind schedule because of the terrific hun resistance, but which was carried through after the divisional commander himself came up to attend conferences to help replan the operation which carried the town. Not far away were Assaro. Leonforte, Castlenuova, Regal-buto and Adrano, all places where the Canadians had made their mark and their name. I went over the ground with one of the officers who had been in the operation at Agira, and he showed me the method of operating and the difficulties which they had encountered and overcome. That assembly place, I can assure the house and the people of Canada, is a dignified and a worthy resting place for those who gave their lives in Sicily. There, in after years, friends can go from Canada and pay tribute to the men who are gathered there, who sleep a warrior's sleep after having truly fought a warrior's fight.
That is the briefest sort of report on my trip. I saw the commanders, General Eisenhower, General Alexander and General Montgomery; I had an opportunity of talking with them, and I want to say that the cordiality, the informative w'av they received and talked with me, and the receptive attitude which they displayed, were things for which I was gratified and for which I thanked them on behalf of Canada. We talked straight from the shoulder. They held nothing back. They told me their plans and I told them ours. I cannot tell them here, but I mention this to remind the committee that of course there must be some things. that we who have the responsibility for these operations would know and would learn, that would influence decisions, which cannot be explained at the present time. So one has to ask the public to withhold conclusions until all the facts are known. I was tremendously thrilled, of course-and perhaps this was the highlight of the trip outside the visit to the troops-to hear the unanimous, enthusiastic and I may say unsolicited testimony which all three of these high-ranking and experienced officers gave with regard to Canadians and their magnificent work as part of their formations. They ware unqualified in their welcome to the Canadians and in praise of their work; if I remember correctly, General Montgomery's tribute was that there were no better troops in any army anywhere.

I have not said anything about the discussions at our forward headquarters in Italy. I visited those headquarters twice, where I had many discussions with regard to administrative matters. There they handle matters affecting our troops right on the ground. Matters concerning personnel, casualties, promotions, supplies and the administrative services are dealt with on the spot. It gave me an opportunity of seeing a well functioning. as I thought, and a well organized headquarters, going concern, in the field of operations.
Among the many things I had to deal with there were three affecting the troops that I might mention. One was mail. Generals may be important; ministers may have some little importance sometimes, but generally speaking the most important man in the unit is the corporal with the mail, and that was impressed upon me time and time again. I want to say to the people of Canada, through this house, that nothing can help keep up the morale of our troops like having mail get to them just as frequently and as quickly as possible. The mail service was not good at the time I was there, far from it; and I want to pay tribute to the Royal Canadian Air Force and to Trans-Canada Air Lines for the work they have done in endeavouring to put on a Canadian service to the Mediterranean. I know it has not- worked perfectly, but that has not been the fault of either the Royal Canadian Air Force or Trans-Canada Air Lines. The route they have to fly has its difficulties, its accidents and its contingencies of weather which of course interfere with uniform and regular deliveries. Mai! is all-important, and I do not mean mail telling of troubles at home; I mean mail which makes the boys realize that we are behind them, which tells the boys the bright side of life here, because believe me they have enough of the drab side in service out there.
Films wore another matter-old films. They complained bitterly about their films being out of date. That condition has been very much improved since then.
The next thing was a paper for the troops. The Maple Leaf was established on January 14. It is a newspaper published in Naples, and goes to all the troops in that area now. It is edited by the services themselves. I have seen the troops and-as I told the newsmen at Algiers-after having seen them, and after knowing something at least of what they have gone through and what they had accomplished, the ground over which they had fought and the successes they had won, I never was as proud of being a Canadian as I was that night.
