Joist one more things-and it has to do with the sombre side of warfare. Speaking of Agira, and the bit of hallowed ground there, the assembling place for our heroic dead, may I humbly put on record the casualties up to January 8. Up to that date casualties in Sicily and Italy totalled: killed in action, 1,079; died of wounds, 272; unclassified deaths, 3, giving a total of 1,354 deaths. Missing were 299; prisoners of war, 86, and wounded, 4,655. Those figures, of course, have grown since January 8.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has spoken of the enormous sum of around three billions of dollars called for by him in the resolution. I think the hearts of Canadians everywhere go out to those homes of which the minister spoke-the thousands of homes in Canada represented in these casualty lists. It is those homes which know the real cost of the war. It is not in dollars and cents. The contribution they make is not found in an income tax schedule. Their gift is of the priceless lives and war wounds of those who. to them, were the dearest on earth.
That, Mr. Chairman, is a brief report of the visit to the troops in Italy. I came back more determined than ever to do my best to see to it that they are well served. Anything one can do, any opportunity one has to be associated with men of that kind is a privilege, and something for which I, speaking for myself, thank God.
Let me speak now of the troops in Canada and deal, if I may, with the question asked the other day by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon). There has been a good deal of discussion with regard to the number of troops in Canada. I wish to make it clear, to put on the record and tell the committee what the situation is in that respect. As I explained last year, our troops are divided into operational troops, non-operational troops, troops in training-and now we have made a fourth division, namely disposal and selection centres, where for the time being men are at depots for the purpose of being discharged or of being posted to other tasks.
Included in those operational troops were the 6th, 7th and 8th divisions, to which I referred last year. The leader of the opposition has asked this question: Why were the 7th and 8th divisions disbanded? And this question: If they were disbanded, why were they ever formed? May I say to him and to the house that I said last year that I hoped we would have a reduction in the number of troops in Canada. In connection with operational troops, at that time we had about
80,000.	We had assessed the situation with respect to possible scales of attack which might
be expected, and those scales of attack had been appraised, along with our friends in the United States who had the same problem there.
Having assessed those scales of attack, the Department of National Defence, and I as minister of that department recommended to the government that we could disband the 7th and 8th divisions, and reorganize the 6th division, because the strategic situation had changed things due to the occupation of the Aleutians.
I think there has been more misrepresentation about the disbanding of the 7th and 8th divisions than perhaps in connection with anything else which has taken place concerning the army. The 7th and 8th divisions were disbanded because it was felt they were not needed longer as operational troops. That is the simple reason. And in disbanding them it was not intended to nor did we discharge physically fit men. The divisions, as divisions, were disbanded, but the men who were in the division either went to other units, to fill them up, or went to the training stream to train and to be fitted for overseas service. N.R.M.A. men in these divisions were sent to other units to relieve general service personnel. Some low-category men were discharged from the service in order that they might fill civilian occupations, and supply civilian needs. It seems to me that was a simple and sensible operation, but it certainly has been misrepresented in this country, and at first at least it was misunderstood in the United States.
I wish to emphasize just that one point, that no man physically fit for overseas service, other than in most exceptional cases, has been discharged, unless on compassionate grounds. The result has been to release more men for overseas service and to raise the average standard of physical fitness in the operational units. That is why the 7th and 8th divisions were disbanded.
Why were they formed? Some hon. members have, I think, very short memories. I want to recall this, that when war broke out with Japan, immediate steps were taken to strengthen the Pacific coast defences. We rushed troops there in the form of extra battalions and thickened our coastal artillery defences. As the Japanese success proceeded- with, I may say, pretty disastrous and alarming rapidity-pressure was increased from all sides to add to those defences in the Pacific coast area.
Pearl Harbor was in December, 1941. In April, 1942, the mobilization of the 7th and Sth divisions was authorized, in addition to the 6th division, and money was subsequently
War Appropriation-Army

voted in this house. And there was not a single voice raised against the authorization for the formation of those two divisions. Two months later the Japanese attacked in the Aleutians. And then the possibility of a direct attack on Canada reached what might be called its zenith. Japanese forces were everywhere in the ascendancy.
In the Aleutians they had established an advance base. That meant an advance base in North America. Then it was not a question of whether those divisions should be mobilized, but how quickly we could get them out there. The pressure of that summer was something which I shall not soon forget. And it was not only the army which was built up to resist that attaek, because there was heavy pressure from all sides on the navy and the air force. I remember very well that increased air protection was urged, and a very large expansion of the air force on the Pacific coast was made.
That is why the 7th and 8th divisions were formed, and I have just told the committee why they were disbanded. I said that the strategic position had changed. By the end of 1942 the pendulum had swung the other way, and with the reoccupation of the Aleutians in August, 1943-remember the date-it was felt that the scale of attack could be changed. We did not lose any time about it. In September we authorized the disbanding of the 7th and 8th divisions. I do not want to make comparisons with other countries, but I do think we as Canadians can feel that we were at least as forward in that as our good neighbours to the south. It was some time after that before the announcement was made by them with regard to a change in their dispositions. Their desire was the same as ours, to release more men for overseas service. That is the situation and that is the answer to my hon. friend.
To-day in Canada we have three brigade groups. One of them consists of the brigade group which was at Kiska. Somebody wdll say. "What do you want them for?" I can only say that we want them because we are advised that there are certain scales of attack which are still a possibility. It is all very well just to say, "Let us put the guns in grease and close up on the two coasts", but I want to tell this committee that on Christmas day there was an alarm on the east coast and everybody was standing by. Shortly after that there was an alarm on the west coast and everybody was standing by. I can imagine what the condemnation would have been had there been nobody at those posts to stand at the alert.

We have a training brigade in the east and we have a few infantry battalions. We have troops in Labrador, Newfoundland, in the Caribbean and in the West Indies, all of which are included with the strength of troops in Canada. It is not as though those operational troops were there for just one purpose. The endeavour has been to make them as flexible as we possibly could, and that flexibility is demonstrated by the fact that they are trained for the defence of Canada, as I have indicated, as well as to provide reinforcements if they are needed overseas. They are trained also-and this applies particularly to the Kiska force-for special duties in the Pacific should action make that necessary and should the decision be made to send them there. I think we have a rather tidy situation. I think we have made the best of what we have. We are still at war and we do not know what the future may hold. I contend that it is good insurance to have these troops trained for whatever role they may be called upon to fill.
I have mentioned Kiska. Fortunately Kiska was an operation which resulted successfully without the firing of a shot as far as the enemy were concerned. But I want to say this for the Kiska force and for the organization of it. No better found, no better trained, no more alert a force ever left Canada than that force which went to Kiska. I want to pay a tribute to the organization of the Pacific command and to headquarters for the way in which that force was organized in a comparatively short time and made ready to go. I want to repeat here the thanks which I expressed to the Hon. Mr. Stimson, United States secretary of state for war, when I wrote to him and expressed our appreciation for the magnificent cooperation which was received in that operation from the officers and men of the United States navy and army. It was a perfect example of team work. The fact that we were able to disband the 7th and 8th divisions was due to the reoccupation of Kiska. We are proud that it was reoccupied by the joint forces of the United States and Canada.
I want now to say a word with regard to non-operational troops in Canada. These are the troops which serve the different establishments which we have in this country. These are the troops which provide the service with respect to ordnance and supplies going overseas. These are the troops which supply the training staffs for the centres for training reinforcements for overseas. They comprise a good many different groups and a great many different arms of the service. I shall not trouble to put them on record at this time, but I ask the committee to think, for

War Appropriation-Army
instance, of ordnance, army service corps, medical corps, provost corps, veterans' guard, staff clerks. There are many places outside of district headquarters and national defence headquarters where these troops are required. They include the depot at Longue Pointe which is operated principally not only for storage but for the concentration and shipment of supplies to the United Kingdom government. Over three thousand men are employed at this depot. Men of these non-operaitional troops are employed in ordnance and ammunition service for other countries. There are dental units to service the navy and the air force, as well as service corps and postal corps for the air force. That gives the committee some idea of the activities of these non-operational troops.
I wish we could cut them down. No one more than the minister would like to see them reduced. We have put a ceiling on them and we are below that ceiling now, but not a great deal. We were able to make a reduction of something like three thousand troops in these non-operational units. That does not sound like a large reduction, but it must be remembered that it was made notwithstanding the fact that we have provided certain new units which had not been required before. I refer to the training brigade on the east coast which is doing such a splendid job in training reinforcements, and certain other units which have been formed for the purpose of doing civilian rather than military work, such as port companies and wood-cutting detachments. There have been increases in certain units which were serving other governments and the navy and air force.
I want to stress the fact that the non-operational troops in Canada, and the whole army in Canada as far as that goes, perform a vital service as a base for both equipment and the providing and training of troops for overseas, as well as the provision of administrative services for both the United Kingdom and the Mediterranean areas. When, we talk about the size of our army we must look at our army as a whole. We must remember that it is one army, one organization, and that a major task for these troops in Canada is to see to it that the men in the line are properly served.
Now I wish to speak of our overseas army in England and perhaps this would be the appropriate time for me to say something regarding the leave of absence which was granted to General McNaughton and which has been the subject of a good deal of comment. On December 27, I issued a statement to the press with regard to General McNaughton as follows:
The Minister of National Defence announced to-day that following the recent illness of
Lieutenant-General A. G. L. McNaughton, medical authorities have advised that he has developed a physical condition which will necessitate freedom from all military responsibility for an extended period.
General McNaughton has advised the government of his inability physically to carry on and has asked to be relieved as soon as possible.
In these circumstances and in view also of the requirements of impending operations, the minister stated that the Canadian government, with great regret, had decided to grant General McNaughton several months' leave of absence from service and to relieve him of command of the First Canadian Army. The minister paid tribute to General McNaughton's outstanding service to Canada and hoped that after a period of rest and recuperation his unusual talents would be available to serve his country in some capacity less exacting than in command of an army in the field.
Lieutenant-General K. Stuart, present chief of the general staff, has been appointed chief of staff at Canadian military headquarters, London, and Major-General P. J. Montague will continue as Major-General in charge of administration at Canadian military headquarters, London, taking that title and as judge advocate general, Canadian army overseas. Pending the appointment of a successor to General McNaughton, Lieutenant-General Stuart has been appointed to the acting command of the First Canadian Army.
The minister stated further that Canadian troops in the Mediterranean had been increased to constitute a Canadian corps under Lieutenant-General H. D. G. Crerar.
The important points were that medical authorities had advised that the general had developed a physical condition which would necessitate freedom from all military responsibility for an extended period and that General McNaughton had advised the government of his inability physically to carry on and had asked to be relieved as soon as possible, and that the government had decided to grant General McNaughton several months leave of absence from service and to relieve him of command of the First Canadian Army.
The advice of the medical authorities was contained in two reports which were transmitted to the Prime Minister on General McNaughton's direction and were also given to me.
The first report came to me about November 29 when I was in the Mediterranean area, and the second when I returned to England about December 10. The reports were as follows:

I feel that the house and the country would like to have that statement on Hansard. It was as follows:
The word that General McNaughton has found it necessary to relinquish the command of the First Canadian Army will be received throughout Canada with feelings of the deepest regret. Especially will this be the case because of the present condition of his health.
General McNaughton's exceptional abilities as a scientist, coupled with his record as a soldier, marked him out as one particularly suited to plan a modern mechanized military force. With this part of Canada's war effort, he has been most intimately connected from day to day through the whole course of the war.
All Cafiada will recall the confidence which General McNaughton helped to inspire in the dark days of 1940. After the withdrawal from Dunkirk, the First Canadian Division was one of the few formations available in Britain equipped with weapons to fight. As General McNaughton's division grew to a corps, and then to an army of two corps, he accepted the growing responsibilities and faced the new problems with the utmost skill and devotion.
Weeks and months and years of waiting made heavy demands upon all the Canadian forces in Britain. They made especially heavy the burden of responsibility upon the army commander. Until now- few will have realized the great strain under which General McNaughton has worked through years of unremitting tension. It is a strain which has been the greater for him through the loss in action of a gallant son.
During General McNaughton's command, the training and organization of Canada's army overseas has been brought to a very high level. The Canadian units w-ho went into action with the Eighth Army in Sicily last July, and who are to-day fighting with such determination in Italy, have won the highest praise for gallantry in action and for stubborn courage and resolution under fire. Some of this praise belongs to General McNaughton. It reflects the fighting spirit which will always be associated with him as commander of Canada's army overseas.
General MeNaughton's health has prevented h in irom carrying on, as he would have wished, until the end of the war. He has, however, the satisfaction of know-ing that his work has been a large factor in contributing to the successes tnus far achieved by Canada's army, and that it w-ill have its part in the supreme -effort needed to attain ultimate victory.
All Canada will wish for General McNaughton a speedy restoration of his health, and that his exceptional abilities and wide experience may-long continue to be at the service of our country.
General McNaughton is now on leave, as recommended by the medical authorities. We are all glad to know that he is making good
improvement, and I repeat most sincerely what I said to him in my letter of December 22, that the only thing for him to do now is to devote all his endeavours to getting well.
I am sure that the house and the country will join in wishing for Mrs. McNaughton and for him, as well as for ourselves, that he may have a speedy and complete recovery' and many years of usefulness in the service of Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have no doubt that with the rumours and so-called "inside", "off the record" reports which are current, there might be a desire on the part of members of the house and others to make inquiries here or elsewhere as to the truth or otherwise of these rumours and reports. We could go into all of this as well as any other matters relating to the subject. I would prefer not to do so because such discussions can, to say the least, do no possible good, especially at times like these.	[DOT]
If you ask me whether General McNaughton and the government were always in absolute agreement in everything, I would undoubtedly answer "no." General McNaughton is a man of strong character and strong opinions. He is no "yes-man". The government is the representative of 'the people of Canada and charged with the responsibility of administering Canada's war effort and the affairs of Canada's army. From what I hear at times, the minister apparently is not a "yes-man" either. That there should be at times divergence of views between the military and the government is inevitable. But I can say that those differences of opinion have not interfered in any way with the loyal carrying out of plans when a decision has been reached. I can say, too, that those differences of opinion have never altered in any way the high regard in which the government holds General McNaughton both as a man and as a soldier.
I can only hope that General McNaughton will be allowed to get the rest and recuperation which he is seeking, free from the worry which a controversy would entail. I hope also that the house and the country will recognize that the important thing at this time is to carry on with the pressing activities of the war and to give wholehearted support to those who are now and who may be charged with the responsibility of leading the Canadian forces in the battle theatres.

Now with regard to the army overseas, in England the work and preparation go on. We have there an army headquarters, army troops and a corps. I want the committee to realize, if I can bring it home to them, just what that means-an army headquarters, army troops and a corps. A corps consists normally of two or three divisions. Then there are corps and divisional troops. We have over there reinforcements, the hospitals, the forestry corps, base installations, ordnance workshops and depots, the Canadian Women's Army Corps, and administrative services. They all have their tasks and they are training to fit into the plan of operations. I had an opportunity, both before I went to North Africa and the Mediterranean area and after I came back, particularly the latter to visit quite a number of units and formations which form the Canadian army overseas in England. I cannot tell this committee how keen they are or how hard they are working to put their years of training and preparation to the test. The waiting time for them is past. At last they can see ahead the prospect of striking the blow which will tell to shorten the war and hasten the day of return.
There is a lot written and a lot said about the army, and with all due respect I am not sure that even this committee understands just what is the composition of our forces overseas.
TMr. Ralston.]
I should like to put on record a very brief explanation of what constitutes that army, so that there will not be the apparent misunderstanding and, I submit, sometimes misrepresentation with regard to that organization.
In the first place-I am dealing with an editorial which I saw the other day-the army overseas does not consist of six or seven divisions. Some editor said that just the other day. Second, the army in Italy does not consist of three divisions. The army that is in England and in Italy consists of one army headquarters, that is officers and other ranks, signallers and so on, having to do with the operational and administrative services and the necessary troops in order to carry on those services. In addition to army headquarters, there are army troops-I will explain that in a moment-two corps headquarters, corps troops, and five divisions. That is the army overseas, both in England and in Italy. I want to make it quite clear that while for organizational purposes we divide the troops into groups, and have troops known as divisional and corps and army and line of communication and G.H.Q. troops, it does not necessarily follow that units included in those groups fight with and serve only the units within that particular group.
Whenever formations are organized, and particularly the larger formations of divisions and corps, it is always necessary to provide, with the units of the division or of the divisions forming the corps, a certain proportion of units which are required to support those formations.
What is a corps? A corps consists of a headquarters, certain corps troops, and two or more divisions. The corps headquarters is so organized that it can direct and administer two or more divisions. Corps troops are provided on the basis of a certain proportion for each division allotted to the corps. Quite often the division itself throws off a certain number of troops of certain units and hands them over to the corps commander in order that he may use them to serve either one division or the other, or both perhaps if they happen to be in the line. It may be signals, it may be artillery, it may be line of communication troops, contributed by the two divisions to the corps headquarters to serve the divisions which are in the line, and if one is in a tough spot, extra corps artillery may be put behind them.
As I have said, we have two corps, each with a headquarters. We have allotted two divisions to one of these corps, the one in Italy, and three to the other. One corps with its two divisions and an armoured formation and an appropriate proportion of army troops is in Italy under the command of Lieutenant-

War Appropriation-Army
General Crerar. The other corps with its three divisions and another armoured formation is in the United Kingdom.
But we have something more in the United Kingdom. This is what seems to confuse people. We have the First Canadian Army headquarters and the remainder of the army troops which have not been allotted to the corps in Italy.
What is an army? I have said that a corps is an organization which administers, supports and directs two or more divisions. An army is an organization consisting of a headquarters, and army troops supporting, servicing, directing two or more corps. The army headquarters and the army troops in England at the present time-let the committee not forget this-were authorized and organized two years ago when we expected major activities across the channel. And there was not a single objection to it at that time. Then what happened?
Until the middle of 1943 the army stayed as a whole in England, because it was represented to us that that was where the job was. Some people said it was because the government were afraid of having the army do any fighting. Other people suggested that it was because the army commander wanted to keep it together. The truth is that the Canadian army overseas was there to be used, in whole or in part, as would best serve the allied cause. As has been said again and again, the army' overseas was kept in England because we were given to understand that that was where it could serve the best in those lean days when Britain had to stand on the defensive. But if we kept these troops in England until the time came to strike across the channel it meant that the whole Canadian contribution in land forces overseas would be thrown into battle without any of them ever having any experience under battle conditions or having heard a shot fired in anger, except the very few who might be attached for short periods to British formations in other theatres. That was the situation which we had to face in the early days because the allies were on the defensive, but it was a situation we could cure when the allies assumed the offensive and we took Steps to do it.
In November, 1942, the North African show came along. Canadians were not in, it. I was in England at the time and went immediately to inquire why, and was given, as I have already stated in the house, what I considered were good and sufficient reasons for not adding a Canadian component to the British and American forces at that time. Once more I underline the flexibility of our
organization, and that our willingness to serve did not mean "all or nothing"; that it meant "in whole or in part."
In the spring the Sicilian operation was planned and the government learned of it in due course. The Canadian government suggested that Canadian troops be employed as part of the force and eventually a request was received for a division. The division went.. It joined the redoubtable Eighth Army. The story of thirty-nine days' fighting in Sicily and six months in Italy is a golden page in Canada's war history.
After prospects faded for activity across the channel in 1943, we sought opportunity to give battle experience to more of our officers and men, not only to another division but to a corps headquarters, corps troops and army troops as well. It would be, we thought, a direct contribution to victory in driving out the enemy, but as well, it would give the Canadian army battle-trained officers and men to be available to be drawn on to help season and steady and inspire our troops in England when their job came.
We pressed for the inclusion of another division and of a corps headquarters in Italy. The arrangement was made. Another division was sent. The corps headquarters was sent, corps and army troops were sent, and to-day we have a self-contained formation on that front as part of the Eighth Army. In England we have the other corps headquarters, corps troops, three divisions and the remainder of the army troops.
As I have said, we have in England army troops and an army headquarters. What do we do with them when we have only one corps remaining in England? The answer is that those who are conducting operations are extremely glad indeed to have that army headquarters there with those army troops in order that they may direct and administer and support the Canadian corps along with other formations of British or other allied troops which may 'be put into the same army organization.
What were the alternatives? Well, there were two. One was to disband the army headquarters and the remainder of the army troops. If we did that it simply meant throwing away the benefit of long training of a highly efficient team at army headquarters and putting our corps in England under some new headquarters completely strange to our personnel and conditions. The disbandment of Canadian army headquarters would simply leave a vacancy in the order of battle of the combined armies, and would require replacement by another headquarters drawn from British or allied sources. It would do no
War Appropriation-Army

good to our common cause to disband a headquarters, which through long training with our troops had become a well coordinated and highly efficient team. By the disbandment of the remainder of the army troops we would to that extent be injuring the common cause, by dispersing trained and hardened fighting and administrative troops, and, at the same time, we would be creating a fresh demand upon the already heavily burdened British or allied forces for exactly the same units which must come from some other source, in order to support our forward formations of corps and divisions.
The other alternative-the first, as I have mentioned, would be to disband the army headquarters and troops-would be to hand this headquarters organization and these army troops over to the allies and let them officer it to suit themselves. We have chosen neither of these alternatives. We propose to keep our army headquarters and our army troops to serve our own Canadian corps in the United Kingdom, and whatever formations of our allies are included with ours. It follows that any allied formations placed under the control of our army headquarters would bring with them the appropriate proportion of corps and army troops for their support.
In a word, we have an army headquarters to control and administer, and army troops to support our corps, and we have the reinforce-_ ments for them. We are going to use that army headquarters and these army troops as a Canadian organization to add to our contribution to victory and to provide the world with further demonstration that Canada is "all-out" in her war effort.
I believe that Canadians will feel that Canada is hitting on all six cylinders with a self-contained corps in Italy with autonomy and self-dependence equivalent to the Canadian corps in the last war. In England we have another corps with its proportion of army troops, and in addition to that we have an army headquarters which we expect will have the distinction of having under its control, not only our own corps and army troops but such other formations and units of the allied countries as may be allotted to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report progress?

Mr. Chairman, in rising to a point of order I think it is only fair that I should give notice of the question that I intended to ask the minister who did not seem to want to answer it this afternoon. My question is whether or not any factors, other than that which he mentioned of ill-health, entered into the resignation of General McNaughton?
I shall deal with that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report progress?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Chairman, I think I should say something about the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and concurred in by the hon. member for Lethbridge, namely, that we should change our procedure this year and by general consent conclude the discussion on the resolution at an early stage.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the minister the unanimous consent to continue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do I need unanimous consent to continue?
If you do, you have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; I think that we are prepared to agree with the suggestion, but I am just a little doubtful whether the discussion would cease as early as it is hoped that it would. However, I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that discussion on the resolution should be short.
Are you prepared to bring down the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not been able to get the house to agree. I have tried to get resolutions out of committee by saying, "Let us talk about this on the bill." Now that someone else proposes it I agree with the proposal, but I have never been able to get the house to agree with me. When we get to the bill we shall do on one section of the bill exactly what for the last three or four years we have done on the resolution; that is, the departments would have to be taken up one by one in order and fully discussed, which, I think, might have the effect of doing away with some duplication, if we can get the resolution reported.
Would the minister include the estimates in a schedule to the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; that is the point I want to make clear.
There is not much use in making a change unless you do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That cannot be done because there must be elasticity in the expenditure .of these funds. In a war you cannot say how much you need for one purpose rather than another purpose. These are estimates at the present time. There must be transfers from one item to another, from one department to another, in a great many cases.

Does that not answer the whole thing? If you are not going to add a schedule, why change the arrangement?

Labour Conditions-Wages Control

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To get rid of some duplication. I suggest to the leader of the opposition that he think about the matter between now and Monday. It depends very much on what he says about it. I am just going along the way I did last year and the year before because the house would not vote the money, they would not pass the resolution giving us billions of dollars unless they had an account of our expenditures of the year before. They never would do it. If they will do this year I shall be very happy.

You would be the first
one to ask the same questions if you were leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know if I would or not.
If you did not you would not be a very good leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not disagreeing with anybody. I am just, saying, if you do agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I am agreeable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

No. I think it depends upon the addition of the schedule.
Mr. GRAYDON; Everything depends upon that.
That is what I had in mind, anyhow.
If you are not going to have the schedule let us go on as we were. I think the decision can be made now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 6.12 p.m.
Monday, February 14, 1944
